screens.title: Recap: Stem Cell Sources
screens.html:
QUICK REVIEW

Recap: Stem Cell Sources

Totipotent - Can become any cell type, including the placenta.

Pluripotent - Can differentiate into any of the three germ layers.

Multipotent - Can only differentiate into a specific family of cells.

screens.title: Stem Cell Potency & Ethics
screens.html:
Stem Cell Potency & Ethics

Question 1:

Which source of stem cells causes the most ethical debate due to the destruction of a blastocyst?

Question 2:

What technological breakthrough allows us to create pluripotent cells from a patient's own skin cells?

Question 3:

Why are multipotent stem cells less attractive for nervous system repair than pluripotent cells?

Answers on the next slide...

screens.title: Stem Cell Potency & Ethics
screens.html:
Stem Cell Potency & Ethics

✅​

Answer 1:

Embryonic Stem Cells (ESCs).

Answer 2:

Induced Pluripotent Stem Cells (iPSCs).

Answer 3:

Their differentiation potential is limited; they may not easily form the specific neurons required.

screens.title: Alzheimer’s Disease (AD)
screens.html:
🔍

Alzheimer’s Disease (AD)

AD is the most common form of dementia. It is a progressive neurodegenerative disease characterized by loss of cognitive function.

Example

Early symptoms include short-term memory loss, followed by decline in language and executive function as the cerebral cortex and hippocampus atrophy.

screens.title: AD Pathophysiology: Plaques and Tangles
screens.html:
AD Pathophysiology: Plaques and Tangles

Two primary proteins drive the destruction of brain tissue in Alzheimer's disease:

Amyloid-β Plaques

Extracellular deposits that interfere with communication at the synapses between neurons.

Tau Tangles

Intracellular proteins that collapse the transport 'tracks' (microtubules) within the axon.

screens.title: Atrophy of the Cerebral Cortex
screens.html:
🔑

Atrophy of the Cerebral Cortex

As neurons die, the overall volume of the brain shrinks. The hippocampus (responsible for forming new memories) is often the first area to show significant damage.

Key point

Because AD affects different parts of the brain simultaneously, CRT is more complex than in localized disorders like Parkinson's.

screens.title: Applying CRT to Alzheimer’s
screens.html:
🧠

Applying CRT to Alzheimer’s

The goal in AD is to replace destroyed neurons in the hippocampus and cortex.

Research focuses on transplanting Neural Stem Cells (NSCs) that can differentiate into new neurons and glial cells.

Remember

New cells must not only survive but also form functional synapses with existing neural networks.

screens.title: Parkinson’s Disease (PD)
screens.html:
Parkinson’s Disease (PD)

PD is a motor system disorder. Unlike AD, it has a very specific focal point: the Substantia Nigra in the midbrain.

Neurons here produce dopamine, a neurotransmitter essential for regulating smooth, purposeful movement.

screens.title: PD Pathophysiology: Loss of Dopamine
screens.html:
🔍

PD Pathophysiology: Loss of Dopamine

Parkinson's involves dopamine neuron death. By symptom onset, 80% are often lost.

Example

Symptoms include resting tremors, muscle rigidity, and bradykinesia (slowed movement).

screens.title: The Perfect Candidate for CRT?
screens.html:
The Perfect Candidate for CRT?

Parkinson's is considered the 'low hanging fruit' for CRT. Why? Because the damage is localized to one specific area and involves one main cell type: Dopaminergic Neurons.

If we can replace these specific cells, we may be able to restore the brain's ability to produce dopamine naturally.

screens.title: Dopaminergic Neuron Replacement
screens.html:
Dopaminergic Neuron Replacement

Induction/Harvest

iPSCs are created from the patient or ESCs are harvested.

Differentiation

Growth factors (like sonic hedgehog) guide stem cells into dopamine neurons.

Transplantation

Cells are injected surgically into the striatum or substantia nigra.

b) Alzheimer's is easier because the plaques and tangles provide clear targets for new stem cells.

screens.title: CLINICAL TRIALS
screens.html:
CLINICAL TRIALS

🤯

Current Clinical Trials

Most CRT for the nervous system is currently in Phase I or II clinical trials. This means we are testing safety and dosage first.

Fun fact

Trials in Japan and the US are already using iPSCs to treat Parkinson's, showing significant improvement in motor control for several patients.

screens.title: Success Story: 2018 Kyoto Trial
screens.html:
Success Story: 2018 Kyoto Trial

Researchers at Kyoto University transplanted 2.4 million dopaminergic precursors into the brain of a PD patient.

The cells were derived from iPSCs, meaning the patient's own genetic profile could be matched to reduce rejection.

screens.title: Risk: Immune Rejection
screens.html:
Risk: Immune Rejection

Embryonic stem cells (ESCs) are genetically distinct from the patient, triggering rejection.

The Problem

Patient immune systems identify transplanted cells as foreign invaders.

The Solution

Use immunosuppressants or patient-derived iPSCs to avoid rejection.

screens.title: CRITICAL CONCERN
screens.html:
CRITICAL CONCERN

⚠️

Risk: Tumorigenesis

Stem cells are defined by their ability to divide rapidly. If they are not fully differentiated before transplant, they can continue to grow uncontrollably.

Watch out

Undifferentiated stem cells can form teratomas—tumours containing various types of tissue like hair, bone, or muscle.

screens.title: Ethical Considerations
screens.html:
Ethical Considerations

While science has progressed, ethical hurdles remain regarding the source of cells.

Status of the human blastocyst.

Potential for cloning or 'designer' humans.

High cost of treatment limiting access.

screens.title: Comparing AD and PD in CRT
screens.html:
Comparing AD and PD in CRT

The success of CRT depends heavily on the nature of the disorder.

Parkinson's

Localized damage; single cell type.

Easier to target.

Alzheimer's

Widespread damage; multiple proteins.

Harder to repair networks.

screens.title: CRT Technical Terms
screens.html:
CRT Technical Terms

In Parkinson's, CRT targets the ____ neurons in the substantia nigra. If these cells are not fully differentiated, they may form tumors called ____. One way to avoid immune rejection is to use ____ which are made from the patient's own tissue.

Word bank 🏦​

pathogens, dopaminergic, amyloid, teratomas, blastocysts, iPSCs

Answers on the next slide...

screens.title: CRT Technical Terms
screens.html:
CRT Technical Terms

In Parkinson's, CRT targets the dopaminergic neurons in the substantia nigra. If these cells are not fully differentiated, they may form tumors called teratomas. One way to avoid immune rejection is to use iPSCs which are made from the patient's own tissue.

Word bank 🏦​

pathogens, dopaminergic, amyloid, teratomas, blastocysts, iPSCs

✅​

screens.title: Glial Cells: The Unsung Heroes
screens.html:
🤯

Glial Cells: The Unsung Heroes

Modern CRT research isn't just about neurons. We are also looking at replacing Glial cells (like astrocytes) which support neurons.

Fun fact

Astrocytes provide the 'infrastructure'—without them, even new neurons will starve and die.

screens.title: The Future of CRT in WA
screens.html:
The Future of CRT in WA

As an ATAR student, you should recognise that CRT is an interdisciplinary field involving biology, ethics, and robotics (for surgical delivery).

The ultimate goal is to move from treating symptoms to providing a curative therapy.

screens.title: Exam Review: Human Endeavour
screens.html:
Exam Review: Human Endeavour

Discuss how the development of induced Pluripotent Stem Cells (iPSCs) has addressed both a biological risk and a significant social/ethical concern in Cell Replacement Therapy.

screens.title: Exam Review: Human Endeavour
screens.html:
Exam Review: Human Endeavour

You might have said...

Biological risk: iPSCs are autologous, eliminating immune rejection and the need for immunosuppressant drugs.

Social/Ethical concern: Because iPSCs are made from adult cells, they do not require the destruction of human embryos, bypassing the debate on blastocyst status.

✅​

screens.title: Lesson Summary
screens.html:
🧠

Lesson Summary

AD involves Amyloid plaques and Tau tangles.

PD involves dopamine loss in the substantia nigra.

CRT aims to replace localized dead cells (PD) or widespread networks (AD).

Major risks: rejection and tumorigenesis.

Remember

iPSCs are the current 'gold standard' for avoiding ethical and immune issues.

questions.title: Written practice
questions.prompt: Compare pluripotent and multipotent stem cells. Give one consideration when selecting a source for therapy.
steps: Pluripotent cells can form cell types from all three germ layers, but do not by themselves have totipotent developmental capacity.
Multipotent cells have a more restricted range of related possible cell types.
Consider the required cell type, rejection risk, growth control, ethical issues or evidence of effectiveness for the intended use.

bank.q: Which potency includes embryonic and extraembryonic cell types?
bank.why: Totipotent cells can contribute to both embryonic and extraembryonic tissues.

bank.q: What are induced pluripotent stem cells?
o: Somatic cells reprogrammed to a pluripotent state
bank.why: Reprogramming can return somatic cells to a pluripotent state.

o: Able to form a limited range of related cell types
Able to form every extraembryonic tissue
bank.why: Multipotent cells can form a restricted range of cell types, commonly within a tissue lineage.
